analysis.body:
The Census BTOS measure for educational services (NAICS 61) shows 35.5% of firms answering yes to using AI in the last two weeks in the latest period, up from 33.8% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023. This is the only measured adoption figure in the source material.

The Department of Education issued the federal guidance, and its inventory lists deployed uses including CAISY for real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation; Grammarly for writing feedback; Otter.AI for transcription; and AWS Bedrock for foundation model applications such as text generation, summarization, conversational AI, personalization, and content creation. Internal uses include generating summaries and outlines, code snippets in multiple languages, R code for data analysis, mock data sets for testing, outreach strategies, and qualifications for public positions. The Department also uses AI to test filters and data loss prevention methods with fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information.

HolonIQ tracks the education economy, including EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning, but the excerpt does not report specific funding totals or vendor shares. The site's course catalog, listed under "Courses and certifications are catalogued here," tracks 13 ai courses, 11 free, with 3 offering companion code. It notes a split between university graduate courses with public materials and industry courses from providers including DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and Andrej Karpathy. The catalog also states it does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

On ROI, the Department of Education's inventory describes CAISY as reducing costs, boosting productivity, and enabling more accurate data-driven decisions, and describes Otter.AI as saving time and improving accessibility. These are product descriptions within the inventory, not independently measured outcomes. The course catalog similarly lacks completion or enrollment data, so the source material offers no verified return-on-investment evidence for education AI deployments.

The regulatory posture is set by the Department of Education, whose guidance frames permissible use, risk, and procurement for US education. The Department's OCIO supports adherence to Federal regulations and responsible and secure usage, in accordance with Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. A reader deciding whether to deploy should weigh the measured adoption rate, the Department's own inventory of practical administrative and instructional uses, and the absence of independent ROI and completion data in the sources.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
